ed.name: Lesotho
ed.stripDate: Due around October 2027 (polling day not yet set)
system: Constitutional monarchy with a parliamentary system: King Letsie III is head of state and the Prime Minister is the leader who commands a majority in the National Assembly. Sam Matekane of the Revolution for Prosperity (RFP) has led a coalition government since November 2022, with the AD and MEC as partners and the support of other parties.

The 120-member National Assembly is elected by a mixed system with one vote: 80 MPs win single-member constituencies by first-past-the-post, and 40 compensatory seats are shared nationally so that each party’s total reflects its share of the vote. Voters do not elect the Prime Minister directly.

No polling day has been set. The current Parliament first sat in late October 2022, and the election is due around October 2027. The IEC says it is preparing for “the 2027 general elections”, and in July 2026 it discussed with the Local Government minister holding National Assembly and local government elections on the same day.

A new IEC led by Rev. Dr John Maphephe took office in early 2026 after months without commissioners, and Tebello Nthakong became Director of Elections in August 2026. Maphephe calls a stable voter register his “first priority” and proposes linking it to national IDs, with alerts to young people when they turn 18. In 2023 the previous commission admitted miscalculating some proportional seats from the 2022 vote.

The SADC-backed reforms are only partly done: the Tenth Amendment (2025) created new oversight bodies, while amendments on floor-crossing, no-confidence votes and the Senate are still pending, and lawyers have challenged the Tenth Amendment in court. In August 2026 the main opposition parties asked SADC to intervene over court rulings they say the government ignores, and the DC suspended its participation in the reforms.

The government declared youth unemployment a national disaster in July 2025, when about 38% of young people were jobless. US tariffs and uncertainty over duty-free access (AGOA) threaten textile jobs, and an activist and a newspaper editor critical of the authorities were arrested in 2025.
ed.status: Party positions in this edition were coded from leaders’ speeches and press conferences, parliamentary debates, opposition letters and the government’s record published up to 18 October 2026; this edition found no 2027 manifestos yet. They have not yet been validated by the parties or by an independent committee. The RFP leads a coalition that includes the AD and MEC. The BAP is split: its leader Nqosa Mahao is in opposition while four of its six MPs stayed with the coalition, so BAP positions here are Mahao’s. Several opposition positions come from the same joint letter to SADC (August 2026).
others: AD · Alliance of Democrats, Ntoi Rapapa (governing coalition partner)
MEC · Movement for Economic Change, Selibe Mochoboroane (governing coalition partner)

PFD, SR, BCM, HOPE, NIP, MPS (one or two seats each in 2022)
and about 45 other registered parties (59 are registered with the IEC)

questions.text: Parliament should order a special audit of the government’s contingency-fund spending before approving new budgets.
questions.ctx: The Contingencies Fund lets the government spend on urgent needs before Parliament votes the money. In February 2026 the Leader of the Opposition asked the Speaker for a special audit and wanted the 2026/27 budget deferred, saying “about 99%” of contingency spending fails constitutional tests. The government says opposition claims of unapproved spending are unproven. The 2025 Tenth Amendment sets new rules on contingencies and supplementary budgets.

ls_dc.n: Mokhothu (Feb 2026) asked the Speaker for a special audit of contingency spending and wanted the budget deferred until it is investigated.

ls_bap.n: Mahao (Feb 2026) said M3.5 billion had been spent without Parliament’s approval.

ls_rfp.n: Government spokesperson Boitelo Rabele (Feb 2026) said the opposition’s claims of unapproved spending were unproven and political.

questions.text: Civil servants should get a pay rise at least equal to inflation, well above the 2% in the 2026/27 budget.
questions.ctx: The 2026/27 budget gave civil servants a 2% pay rise, while the opposition put inflation at about 4.5–4.7%. A bigger rise would protect public workers’ buying power but increase the public wage bill at a time of tight budgets. The ABC proposes 15%.

ls_rfp.n: The government’s 2026/27 budget set a 2% civil-service raise.

ls_dc.n: Mokhothu (Feb 2026) said 2% is too low with inflation at 4.5–4.7%.

ls_abc.n: Kabi (Apr 2026) called for a 15% public-sector pay rise instead of 2%.

questions.text: The old-age pension should rise by far more than the M50 increase planned by the government.
questions.ctx: According to the ABC, the government planned a M50 increase to the old-age pension. The ABC wants M250 and says it can be paid for with SACU revenue, Lesotho Highlands water royalties and taxes. The government has to weigh higher pensions against other spending.

ls_rfp.n: The government planned a M50 pension increase, according to the ABC (April 2026).

ls_abc.n: Kabi (Apr 2026) asked for a M250 increase instead of M50.

questions.text: The budget for international trips by ministers, MPs and officials should be cut by half.
questions.ctx: A parliamentary committee report in March 2025 showed the budget for international trips rose by 102% in 2024/25 and 72% in 2025/26. Two governing-party MPs moved to cut it by 50%. Supporters say the trips waste scarce money; LCD leader Mothetjoa Metsing argued for case-by-case decisions instead of a blanket cut.

ls_rfp.n: Two RFP backbench MPs moved the 50% cut in March 2025, while the RFP-led government’s own travel budget had risen sharply.

ls_dc.n: DC MP Thabiso Lekitla (Mar 2025) questioned whether officials need to fly business class.

ls_bnp.n: Mofomobe (Mar 2025) said “benchmarking” trips abroad cannot be justified.

questions.text: The agriculture budget should be raised sharply, even if money has to be moved away from roads and other infrastructure.
questions.ctx: The 2026/27 budget cut agriculture from M1.3 billion to M1.1 billion. The ABC says money should be shifted from infrastructure to reach about M5 billion for farming. Supporters say farming can create jobs for young people and improve food supply; others say infrastructure also creates jobs and links farms to markets.

ls_rfp.n: The government’s 2026/27 budget reduced agriculture spending to M1.1 billion.

ls_abc.n: Kabi (Feb 2026) said the cut means the government “shot itself in the foot” and proposed moving infrastructure money to reach M5 billion for agriculture.

nd.ls_dc: Mokhothu criticised fertiliser shortages in February 2026 but proposed no budget figure.

questions.text: Small fields should be grouped into large, commercially run “block farming” schemes to raise farm output.
questions.ctx: Only about 11% of Lesotho’s land is arable, according to the ABC. Block farming pools neighbouring fields so they can be ploughed, fertilised and sold together. Supporters say pooling allows machines and larger sales; critics worry families could lose control over their land.

ls_abc.n: Kabi (2025) proposed block farming and keeping land for agriculture rather than housing.

ls_rfp.n: Deputy Prime Minister Nthomeng Majara (July 2026) said agriculture must be commercialised. This edition found no specific government plan for block farming.

questions.text: The government’s youth jobs plan (public works, graduate placements in the National Volunteer Corps, and public contracts reserved for young people) is the right way to tackle youth unemployment.
questions.ctx: In July 2025 the government declared a two-year state of disaster over unemployment; about 38% of young people were jobless. The Prime Minister pledged 70,000 youth job opportunities (later reported as 62,000) in public works, farming, energy, sanitation and ICT, and the 2026/27 budget added 2,500 graduate placements. Opposition parties say the numbers are not credible and that the plan relies on the public sector.

ls_rfp.n: Matekane (June 2025) pledged at least 70,000 youth job opportunities and reserved part of public procurement for young people, women and people with disabilities.

ls_dc.n: Mokhothu (June 2025): “the government claims it will employ 70,000 youth. That is simply not true.”

ls_abc.n: The ABC’s strategic plan (Feb 2026) says the jobs plan relies mainly on the public service and proposes youth corporations instead.

ls_bap.n: Mahao (Feb 2026) said more than 20,000 jobs had been lost since the government took office and accused it of using handouts “to buy loyalty”.

questions.text: Every ministry should set aside a fixed share of its budget for youth job creation.
questions.ctx: Under the July 2025 state of disaster, the government told ministries to devote 2% of their budgets to job creation. The ABC wants each ministry to set aside M20 million for youth jobs. Critics of earmarking say it can take money from core services such as health or schools.

ls_rfp.n: The government’s July 2025 disaster declaration told ministries to put 2% of their budgets into job creation.

ls_abc.n: Kabi (2025) proposed that each ministry set aside M20 million for youth jobs.

questions.text: Minimum wages for textile and factory workers should rise much faster than inflation, even if factory owners object.
questions.ctx: From 1 April 2026 the government raised minimum wages by 4% for textile and factory workers, 3% in the rest of the private sector and 4.5% for other categories, after agreement between employers and workers on the wages advisory board. Textile factories employ about 30,000 people and face US tariffs. Supporters of bigger rises say wages are too low; employers warn that higher costs could push factories out.

ls_rfp.n: Labour Minister Tšeliso Mokhosi announced a 4% rise for textile and factory workers from April 2026, agreed with employers and workers.

ls_abc.n: Kabi (2025) called for higher factory wages, recalling that an ABC-led government raised the lowest wage from M1,500 to over M2,000.

questions.text: Mining companies should pay VAT on the machinery and equipment they import, which is currently zero-rated.
questions.ctx: A VAT Amendment Bill to tax imported mining equipment, which is currently zero-rated, was revived in the current Parliament; opposition MPs say the governing side defeated it. The Minister of Energy and Mining says the tax would raise costs and could force mines to close; supporters say mines should contribute more to public revenue.

ls_rfp.n: Minister of Energy and Mining Lejone Mpotjoane (June 2026) said the VAT bill would raise mining costs and could close mines.

ls_bap.n: Mahao (June 2026) criticised the bill’s defeat and alleged that mine owners had lobbied MPs against it.

nd.ls_dc: The DC criticised the government’s record on diamond benefits (June 2026); this edition found no separate DC statement on the VAT bill.

questions.text: A large share of Lesotho’s diamonds should be cut and polished in the country before export, following Botswana’s example.
questions.ctx: Cutting and polishing diamonds at home (beneficiation) adds value and skilled jobs before export. In June 2026, after talks in Botswana, the Prime Minister said diamonds should benefit citizens, and the Minister of Energy and Mining promised a new Mining Bill to increase local benefits. Opposition parties say the government has done little in four years; critics of strict local-processing rules say they can deter investors.

ls_rfp.n: Matekane (June 2026) said diamonds should benefit citizens, and his minister promised a Mining Bill for more local benefits, without a firm commitment to local cutting.

ls_dc.n: Mokhothu (June 2026) criticised four years of government inaction on beneficiation.

ls_bap.n: Mahao (June 2026) pointed to Botswana’s model of cutting and polishing at home.

ls_bnp.n: Mofomobe (June 2026) called the Prime Minister’s pledge “bluffing” and wants a bigger state shareholding in the mines and a diamond auction house.

questions.text: The government should subsidise petrol, diesel and paraffin far more heavily, paid for with SACU revenue and water royalties.
questions.ctx: By April 2026 fuel prices had jumped (petrol up about M6.70–7.35 a litre, diesel M13.10, paraffin M13.30). The government announced a subsidy of M2 a litre for petrol and diesel and M5 for paraffin. The ABC wants a much bigger subsidy and national fuel and food reserves; critics of subsidies say they are costly and help car owners more than the poorest.

ls_rfp.n: Matekane announced a limited subsidy of M2 a litre for petrol and diesel and M5 for paraffin (2026).

ls_abc.n: Kabi (Apr 2026) asked the Speaker to recall Parliament to direct the government to subsidise fuel, paid for with SACU revenue, water royalties and taxes.

questions.text: Lesotho should press South Africa for free movement, so that Basotho can live and work there without temporary permits.
questions.ctx: Many Basotho live or work in South Africa, and anti-immigrant violence there in 2026 forced some to return home. The BNP wants a permanent arrangement like those between small European states and their neighbours, saying most Basotho do not qualify for South African work permits; the DC wants free movement of people, goods and services. The government says it has cut passport waiting times and that Lesotho must create jobs at home.

ls_bnp.n: Mofomobe (Aug 2025) called for a permanent immigration arrangement with South Africa, citing San Marino, the Vatican and Andorra, instead of temporary permits.

ls_dc.n: Mokhothu (Aug 2025) called for free movement of people, goods and services and for Basotho to cross without passport stamps beyond the 90-day limit.

nd.ls_rfp: Matekane (July 2026) said passports are now issued in four days and that “the most sustainable solution is to create home-based opportunities”; this edition found no government position on a free-movement deal.

questions.text: SADC should intervene in Lesotho over the government’s failure to comply with court rulings.
questions.ctx: In August 2026 the DC leader wrote to the SADC chair, in a letter co-signed by the ABC, BNP, BAP and smaller parties, listing court rulings they say the government ignored: the suspension of the Director of Public Prosecutions, the reinstatement of the revenue commissioner, 77 National Security Service officers expelled unlawfully, and others. The SADC summit communiqué did not mention the complaint. The Prime Minister says there is no contempt where courts did not expressly order a remedy.

ls_rfp.n: Matekane (Aug 2026) rejected the contempt claims and urged the opposition to return to the reforms table.

ls_dc.n: Mokhothu wrote the 3 August 2026 letter to the SADC chair, Zimbabwe’s President Emmerson Mnangagwa.

ls_abc.n: The ABC co-signed the August 2026 letter to SADC.

ls_bap.n: The BAP co-signed the August 2026 letter to SADC.

ls_bnp.n: The BNP co-signed the August 2026 letter to SADC.

questions.text: The government should organise and pay for the return of Basotho fleeing anti-immigrant violence anywhere in South Africa.
questions.ctx: In mid-2026 anti-immigrant violence in South Africa pushed some Basotho to return home. The government organised buses, but only from Durban, according to the BNP, which wants repatriation from all parts of South Africa. The Prime Minister says the passport backlog has been cleared so that Basotho can travel with documents.

ls_bnp.n: Mofomobe (July 2026) demanded repatriation from across South Africa, not only Durban.

ls_rfp.n: The government ran buses for returning Basotho, which the BNP says only covered Durban.

questions.text: To protect textile jobs, Lesotho’s top trade priority should be negotiating with Washington for lower tariffs and continued AGOA access.
questions.ctx: In 2025 the United States announced a 50% tariff on Lesotho’s exports, paused it, and set it at 15% from August 2025. Textile factories, which employ about 30,000 people, depend on duty-free access to the US under AGOA, which had been extended by one year by early 2026. Others argue that Lesotho should instead find new markets, including in Africa under the AfCFTA.

ls_rfp.n: Trade Minister Mokhethi Shelile (Aug 2025) said Lesotho would keep negotiating for minimum tariffs and that the relationship “needs continuous nurturing”.

ls_dc.n: Mokhothu (Apr 2025) urged diplomatic engagement with Washington, but also an emergency economic council and new markets, including the AfCFTA.

ls_bnp.n: Mofomobe (Sep 2025) wrote to the US ambassador to help keep Lesotho eligible for AGOA, asking Washington to press the government on governance.

questions.text: Opposition parties are right to stay out of the national reforms process until the government complies with court rulings.
questions.ctx: The SADC-backed reforms aim to end years of political instability. The Tenth Amendment was passed in 2025, and the government plans a National Reforms Implementation Authority to pass its enabling laws within 18 months. In August 2026 the DC suspended its participation over the rule-of-law dispute, and the Prime Minister appealed to the opposition to return. Critics of the boycott say reforms need all parties; supporters say the government must first respect the courts.

ls_dc.n: Mokhothu (Aug 2026): “Until the government changes, we will continue to suspend our participation in the reforms process.”

ls_rfp.n: Matekane (Aug 2026) appealed to opposition parties to return to the reforms table.

ls_abc.n: The ABC co-signed the August 2026 letter, which threatened to stop taking part in reform meetings.

ls_bap.n: The BAP co-signed the August 2026 letter, which threatened to stop taking part in reform meetings.

ls_bnp.n: The BNP co-signed the August 2026 letter, which threatened to stop taking part in reform meetings.

questions.text: The National Assembly should accept the Senate’s demands, including a bigger Senate and a Paramount Chief post, to unblock the constitutional reforms.
questions.ctx: Parts of the reform package have been stuck between the National Assembly and the Senate (upper house). In 2025 the Senate held back amendments, reportedly seeking an expanded Senate and a Paramount Chief post, and the Law Minister withdrew the Eleventh Amendment (on floor-crossing and no-confidence votes) to redraft it with the Senate’s submissions. According to the BNP, the National Assembly had already rejected many of the chiefs’ proposals.

ls_bnp.n: Mofomobe (2025) accused the Senate of holding the reforms “hostage” to pressure the National Assembly.

ls_rfp.n: Law Minister Richard Ramoeletsi agreed in 2025 to withdraw and redraft the Eleventh Amendment to include Senate submissions, while the RFP-led National Assembly had rejected Senate expansion, according to the BNP.

questions.text: Electoral commissioners should be appointed without waiting for court appeals by unsuccessful applicants to be decided.
questions.ctx: Lesotho went months without electoral commissioners while two unsuccessful applicants challenged the recruitment in court. The government said the appeal did not stop the process, and a new commission led by John Maphephe took office in early 2026. Waiting for courts protects fair recruitment; acting quickly lets the IEC prepare elections.

ls_rfp.n: Law Minister Ramoeletsi (Jan 2026): “The case before the courts does not stay the process.”

ls_bnp.n: Mofomobe (Jan 2026) petitioned the Council of State, calling the constitutional wording “peremptory”, and threatened court action over the delay.

ls_dc.n: The DC (Jan 2026) warned that the delay threatened the integrity of the electoral system.

questions.text: An independent audit should review all government tenders awarded since 2022.
questions.ctx: Opposition parties accuse the government of steering tenders (for roads, seeds and fertiliser, and airport works) to people close to ministers. Parliament’s Public Accounts Committee has recommended action against a minister over a contract linked to his former company. The Prime Minister says anyone with evidence of corruption should bring it forward and offenders will be prosecuted.

ls_dc.n: Mokhothu (Aug 2025) promised an audit of tenders if the DC wins and alleged that seed, fertiliser and airport tenders went to ministers and MPs.

ls_bap.n: Mahao (Feb 2026) said M22 million meant for factories at Ha-Belo was missing.

nd.ls_rfp: Matekane (June 2025) said anyone with evidence should bring it and offenders would be expelled and prosecuted; this edition found no RFP position on a general tender audit.

questions.text: Ministers, including the Prime Minister, should be barred from any business dealings with the state or with mining companies while in office.
questions.ctx: Opposition parties say some ministers do business with their own ministries, and the BNP has objected to the Prime Minister negotiating with mining companies. The Tenth Amendment entrenched an independent anti-corruption commission in the Constitution. Supporters of a strict ban say it prevents conflicts of interest; others say it could keep experienced business people out of government.

ls_bnp.n: Mofomobe (Sep 2025) told the US ambassador that some ministers have business dealings with their own ministries, calling it a governance concern.

ls_dc.n: Mokhothu (June 2025) called the cabinet a “tender committee” and accused ministers of profiting from public contracts.

nd.ls_rfp: Matekane (June 2025) said ministers would be expelled and prosecuted if evidence of corruption is produced; this edition found no RFP position on a business ban.

questions.text: The police should allow peaceful protests, including about job losses, instead of refusing permits.
questions.ctx: From June 2025 the authorities refused permits for protests, including over textile job losses, according to Amnesty International. Supporters of restrictions say protests can turn violent; critics say peaceful assembly is a basic right. The BNP told the US ambassador that limits on demonstrations could cost Lesotho its AGOA trade benefits.

ls_rfp.n: Under the Matekane government, protest permits were refused from June 2025, according to Amnesty International.

ls_bnp.n: Mofomobe (Sep 2025) listed restrictions on the right to demonstrate among the governance failures putting AGOA at risk.

questions.text: Activists and journalists should never face criminal charges, such as sedition, for criticising the government.
questions.ctx: In June 2025 activist and lawyer Tšolo Thakeli was arrested after posting a video criticising the Prime Minister’s handling of unemployment and was charged with sedition, later with incitement. In August 2025 the anti-corruption agency (DCEO) arrested the editor of the Lesotho Times and later dropped the case. Supporters of such laws say they protect public order; critics say they intimidate critics.

ls_rfp.n: Under the current government, police charged activist Tšolo Thakeli with sedition in 2025 and the DCEO detained a newspaper editor, later dropping the case.

ls_bnp.n: Mofomobe (Sep 2025) called the detention of a Lesotho Times journalist an attack on press freedom.

questions.text: The army should be deployed to stop killings by famo gangs.
questions.ctx: Rival famo music groups have been linked to repeated killings. In May 2024 the government banned 12 famo groups and gazetted them as terrorist organisations, and the Prime Minister told the army commander to end the killings “by any means necessary”. Critics said security forces must act within the law and warned against militarising community safety.

ls_rfp.n: Matekane (Aug 2024) ordered the army to end famo killings “by any means necessary”.

ls_dc.n: Mokhothu (Aug 2024) said security agencies must act “within the perimeters of law”, without rejecting a deployment outright.

questions.text: When courts find that the government suspended or dismissed someone unlawfully, it should reinstate that person even if the ruling does not expressly order it.
questions.ctx: Courts ruled the suspension of the Director of Public Prosecutions unlawful and, according to the opposition, found that 77 National Security Service officers were expelled unlawfully. The Prime Minister argues that where a court did not expressly order reinstatement, there is no contempt, and points to cases still before the courts. Opposition parties say ignoring rulings undermines the rule of law.

ls_rfp.n: Matekane (Aug 2026) said the Constitutional Court did not expressly order the DPP’s reinstatement and cited matters still before the courts.

ls_dc.n: Mokhothu’s August 2026 letter to SADC lists the DPP’s suspension and the expelled security officers among rulings the government ignored.

ls_abc.n: The ABC co-signed the August 2026 letter.

ls_bap.n: The BAP co-signed the August 2026 letter.

ls_bnp.n: The BNP co-signed the August 2026 letter.
